item.title: Koroi takes People’s Choice Award
item.description: MISS Grace Roads, Keren Koroi, has apparently taken out the People’s Choice Award after receiving about 7,900 votes online. Ms Koroi received strong support from Navua, with supporters sharing and liking her posts in large numbers ahead of the announcement.
item.content:encoded:
MISS Grace Roads, Keren Koroi, has apparently taken out the People’s Choice Award after receiving about 7,900 votes online.

Ms Koroi received strong support from Navua, with supporters sharing and liking her posts in large numbers ahead of the announcement.

The 21-year-old has strong ties to the town, having lived in Navua since her primary school days at J.N. Jokhan Memorial Primary School.

She later attended Vashist Muni College, where she served as head girl in 2023.

Coming in a close second was Miss MHCC & Carpenters Tower, Sala Korosaya, who received about 7,700 votes and 635 shares.

The People’s Choice result was announced as members of the public turned out in numbers along central Suva despite gloomy weather to witness the Hibiscus float procession at 11am today.

item.title: Tikolevu appointed to FNPF board
item.description: Former Chief Executive Officer of the Fiji Revenue and Customs Authority (FRCA) and former Fiji High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, Mr. Jitoko Tikolevu, has been appointed to the Board of the Fiji National Provident Fund (FNPF) by the Minister for Finance, in accordance with Section 7(1) of the FNPF Act. Mr. Tikolevu’s appointment is effective from 2 September 2026 for a term of four years.
item.content:encoded:
Former Chief Executive Officer of the Fiji Revenue and Customs Authority (FRCA) and former Fiji High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, Mr. Jitoko Tikolevu, has been appointed to the Board of the Fiji National Provident Fund (FNPF) by the Minister for Finance, in accordance with Section 7(1) of the FNPF Act.

Mr. Tikolevu’s appointment is effective from 2 September 2026 for a term of four years.

He brings more than four decades of experience in public administration, taxation, revenue management, policy development, and diplomacy to the Fund. His distinguished career began in the Fiji Civil Service in 1981, before progressing through senior roles in the Auditor General’s Office, Inland Revenue Department, and the Fiji Revenue and Customs Authority.

Mr. Tikolevu served as Chief Executive Officer of FRCA from 2007 to 2015, leading significant fiscal and organizational reforms that enhanced revenue collection, strengthened operational efficiency, and contributed to the agency receiving the Prime Minister’s Service Excellence Award in 2014.

He holds a Diploma in Business Studies from the Fiji Institute of Technology, a Bachelor of Arts in Business Studies from the University of the South Pacific, and a Master of Taxation from the University of Auckland.

Throughout his career, Mr. Tikolevu has held several prominent governance and leadership positions, including Deputy Chairman of the Fiji Development Bank and Investment Fiji Boards, Chairman of the Oceania Customs Organisation Board, and Chairman of the Pacific Islands Tax Administrators Association. He also played a key role in negotiating double taxation agreements between Fiji and several international partners.

Most recently, he served as Fiji’s High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, where he represented Fiji’s interests and strengthened diplomatic and economic ties with key international partners.

FNPF welcomes Mr Tikolevu to the Board. His extensive experience in leadership, governance, public finance and strategic policy will complement the Board’s existing capabilities and support the Fund’s long-term strategic objectives.

item.title: NEC recruitment not based on favouritism, says Ministry
item.description: The Ministry was responding to allegations circulating on TikTok concerning recruitment through the National Employment Centre (NEC), including the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme. It said recruitment is conducted under established bilateral arrangements, programme guidelines and selection frameworks designed to ensure transparency and fairness.
item.content:encoded:
The Ministry was responding to allegations circulating on TikTok concerning recruitment through the National Employment Centre (NEC), including the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme.

It said recruitment is conducted under established bilateral arrangements, programme guidelines and selection frameworks designed to ensure transparency and fairness.

The Ministry said approved employers select workers from the pool of NEC-registered candidates who are work-ready and available.

While employers may identify potential workers through referrals, including recommendations from existing employees, referred candidates must still meet the required registration, assessment and recruitment criteria.

The Ministry said employers ultimately make hiring decisions based on their operational requirements and the suitability of candidates.

Candidates may be assessed on their skills, qualifications, experience, physical capability, police clearance, medical fitness and work-readiness, depending on the job requirements.

The Ministry also warned workers about individuals allegedly providing unauthorised advice or seeking payments, commissions or a share of workers’ compensation or WorkCover settlements.

Workers have been urged to verify the identity and authority of anyone claiming to represent the Ministry and report suspicious approaches through official channels.

The Ministry said allegations of corruption, favouritism or misconduct should be supported by credible evidence and encouraged anyone with information to submit it to the appropriate authorities.

It said it remains committed to transparent, accountable and merit-based recruitment while protecting the welfare of Fijians working overseas.

item.title: Aussies paid for my Palau trip, says Seruiratu
item.description: Seruiratu said he is not in Palau as part of the Fiji Government delegation to the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting. Instead, he is attending in his capacity as the Pacific Envoy for the Oceans for COP31 , where he is supporting efforts to elevate the ocean-climate nexus and promote Pacific priorities ahead of the UN climate conference.
item.content:encoded:
Seruiratu said he is not in Palau as part of the Fiji Government delegation to the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting.

Instead, he is attending in his capacity as the Pacific Envoy for the Oceans for COP31 , where he is supporting efforts to elevate the ocean-climate nexus and promote Pacific priorities ahead of the UN climate conference.

He said all costs associated with his participation are being covered by the Australian Government , and not the Fiji Government or Fijian taxpayers.

Seruiratu said his participation should not be interpreted as support for any particular recommendation arising from Fiji’s constitutional review process.

He said political differences should not prevent constructive engagement on matters affecting Fiji and the Pacific.

“Being in Opposition does not mean opposing every national or regional initiative simply because the Government is involved,” Seruiratu said.

He maintained that the Opposition would continue to scrutinise and hold the Government accountable while contributing to initiatives that advance Fiji’s national and regional interests.

Seruiratu said Fiji’s national interest must come before personalities, political speculation and political point-scoring.

item.title: FIji Navy begins hydrographic work to support forward operating base in Malau
item.description: Naval officers and sailors from the Hydrographic Department have been deployed to conduct the work, which will provide accurate information on waterways and seabed conditions to support safe navigation and future maritime infrastructure development. The deployment forms part of wider Republic of the Fiji Military Forces initiatives to enhance Forward Operating Base capabilities and a whole-of-gove
item.content:encoded:
Naval officers and sailors from the Hydrographic Department have been deployed to conduct the work, which will provide accurate information on waterways and seabed conditions to support safe navigation and future maritime infrastructure development.

The deployment forms part of wider Republic of the Fiji Military Forces initiatives to enhance Forward Operating Base capabilities and a whole-of-government effort to improve maritime infrastructure, navigation safety and operational efficiency in Vanua Levu.

The hydrographic data will support safe vessel movement, maritime operations and the future development of ports and coastal infrastructure.

The work is also aligned with the National Development Plan’s objective of strengthening infrastructure and improving port services for government agencies, commercial operators and communities in the Northern Division.

The Fiji Navy says the deployment demonstrates its commitment to supporting national development, maritime safety and Fiji’s economic security.

item.title: Canberra residence to be restored, not sold, says Ditoka
item.description: Responding to questions raised on social media, Ditoka said the Canberra property was inherited in a condition that was not considered habitable and requires significant work to meet the standards expected of a Head of Mission’s residence. He said similar deterioration had been found at Fiji’s overseas properties in London and Brussels, while the former residence in Wellington had deteriorated to
item.content:encoded:
Responding to questions raised on social media, Ditoka said the Canberra property was inherited in a condition that was not considered habitable and requires significant work to meet the standards expected of a Head of Mission’s residence.

He said similar deterioration had been found at Fiji’s overseas properties in London and Brussels, while the former residence in Wellington had deteriorated to the point where Government eventually sold it and purchased another property.

Ditoka said Canberra had been included in a restoration programme proposed for the current financial year but did not receive funding after Government was forced to tighten expenditure because of the fuel supply crisis and its impact on public finances.

He said restoration funding was instead prioritised for the London Chancery, Fiji House and the Brussels property.

“Canberra is the next major overseas property work we intend to undertake in the next financial year,” Ditoka said.

He said Fiji should be cautious about selling the Canberra residence, noting that it was purchased for AUD852,500 in 2001 and could now be worth several million dollars.

Ditoka said deterioration alone was not sufficient reason to dispose of a valuable State asset.

“The question is not what quick return we can get by selling it today, but what makes better financial sense for Fiji over the longer term,” he said.

He added that if future financial assessments showed that selling the property was the better option, Government should consider it.

Ditoka also said the current accommodation for the Fiji High Commissioner in Canberra is within Government financial policies and regulations and has been budgeted for.

He said the Government would restore overseas properties progressively within available funding while protecting the value of State assets.

item.title: FTUC attacks foreign worker rule changes
item.description: THE Fiji Trades Union Congress has launched a blistering attack on Government’s decision to temporarily ease immigration requirements for employers bringing foreign workers into Fiji, warning the move could come at the expense of local jobs and workers’ rights. FTUC says the changes, which include waivers on proving that workers are unavailable locally and requirements for skills understudy, were
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Trades Union Congress has launched a blistering attack on Government’s decision to temporarily ease immigration requirements for employers bringing foreign workers into Fiji, warning the move could come at the expense of local jobs and workers’ rights.

FTUC says the changes, which include waivers on proving that workers are unavailable locally and requirements for skills understudy, were made without consultation or studies on their impact.

The union claims employers are increasingly turning to foreign workers because they can be made to work longer hours without overtime payments or other employment benefits.

FTUC general secretary Felix Anthony said the lack of oversight over foreign workers was particularly concerning, alleging some were living in poor and “unfit” conditions while facing exploitation with limited avenues for redress.

The union also questioned whether Government agencies have enough resources to monitor work permits, employment conditions, contracts and visa expiry dates amid the growing influx of foreign workers.

FTUC said the decision appeared “ad-hoc” and accused the Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation of successfully lobbying for the changes without adequate consultation with workers’ representatives.

While acknowledging that some industries require overseas labour, FTUC is calling for tripartite consultations involving Government, employers and workers before further decisions are made.

It warned that prioritising foreign labour without safeguards could undermine decent employment opportunities for Fijians and push more locals to seek work overseas.

item.title: Minor electoral breaches should not be criminalised, says CDD
item.description: THE Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026 introduces penalties for conduct that should not necessarily be treated as criminal offences, according to Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD). CDD chief executive officer Nilesh Lal told the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights that Parliament should instead establish three categories of electoral offences, separating minor administrative bre
item.content:encoded:
THE Electoral (Amendment) Bill 2026 introduces penalties for conduct that should not necessarily be treated as criminal offences, according to Centre for Democracy and Dialogue (CDD).

CDD chief executive officer Nilesh Lal told the Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights that Parliament should instead establish three categories of electoral offences, separating minor administrative breaches from conduct that threatens the integrity of elections.

Mr Lal said the proposed legislation’s two categories, illegal electoral practice and corrupt electoral practice, were an improvement but did not go far enough.

He recommended a third category for administrative infringements, covering matters such as late filing, minor labelling errors, correctable form defects and other low-harm procedural breaches.

“These should ordinarily attract a warning, a direction to correct the issue, or a modest administrative or civil penalty, with no imprisonment,” Mr Lal said.

“The second category, illegal electoral practice, would cover deliberate or repeated breaches of electoral rules that cause genuine regulatory harm.

“The most serious category, corrupt electoral practices, should be reserved for conduct such as bribery, treating, undue influence, personation, ballot tampering and serious misuse of State resources.”

Mr Lal said the current system treated fundamentally different conduct through the same criminal lens, with severe penalties applying to technical or administrative failures.

He said an administrative mistake should not be treated in the same way as bribery or deliberate interference with an election.

CDD also raised concerns over what it described as extraordinary powers given to election administration, restrictions on civil society and research, and limits on political expression and public debate.

“CDD is not seeking to dismantle the electoral legislation, but asking Parliament to preserve what works, liberalise unnecessary restrictions and correct poorly drafted provisions.”
